title: Binary Search
description: Learn how Binary Search repeatedly halves a sorted search space and why logarithmic reduction makes searching extremely efficient.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Binary Search is an efficient searching algorithm used to locate an element inside a sorted array.

Instead of checking elements one by one, Binary Search repeatedly finds the middle element, compares it with the target, and removes half of the remaining search space.

This repeated halving makes Binary Search dramatically faster than Linear Search for large datasets. The algorithm is one of the most important examples of Divide and Conquer thinking because it aggressively reduces problem size at every step.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Matters
sections.content:
Searching is one of the most common operations in computing. Large systems constantly locate records, files, usernames, database entries, and indexed values.

Sequential searching becomes expensive as datasets grow larger. Binary Search improves scalability by repeatedly eliminating half of the remaining search space after every comparison.
bullets: It scales efficiently for massive datasets.
It demonstrates Divide and Conquer thinking.

sections.title: Important Requirement — Sorted Data
sections.content:
Binary Search only works correctly when the data is sorted.

For example, the array [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12] allows the algorithm to safely eliminate half of the remaining search space after each comparison because the ordering provides meaningful information.

If the array is unsorted, comparisons lose meaning and the algorithm may discard the wrong section. This makes Binary Search unreliable on unordered data.

sections.title: Core Idea of Binary Search
sections.content:
Binary Search repeatedly divides the problem in half.

The algorithm finds the middle element, compares it with the target, removes the unnecessary half, and repeats the process on the remaining section.

This reduction continues until the target is found or the search space becomes empty. Every step dramatically shrinks the remaining workload.

sections.title: Understanding the Search Pointers
sections.content:
Binary Search commonly uses three important positions called low, high, and mid.

The low pointer marks the beginning of the search range. The high pointer marks the end of the search range. The mid pointer represents the middle element currently being checked.

Initially, low starts at index 0 and high starts at the last index. The midpoint is calculated from the current low and high positions. The middle value determines whether the algorithm searches left or right.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Example
sections.content:
Suppose we search for 11 inside the sorted array [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15].

The middle element is 7. Since 11 is greater than 7, the algorithm eliminates the entire left half.

The remaining search space becomes [9, 11, 15]. The new middle element is 11, so the target is found immediately.

This example demonstrates how Binary Search rapidly reduces the amount of work through repeated halving.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Is Fast
sections.content:
The most powerful feature of Binary Search is search space reduction. Every comparison removes 50 percent of the remaining elements.

Suppose a dataset contains 1,000,000 elements. After one comparison, only 500,000 remain. After another comparison, only 250,000 remain. The workload shrinks extremely quickly.

This repeated halving creates logarithmic growth, which scales very efficiently for large inputs.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: Binary Search implementations must correctly update search pointers and repeatedly reduce the search space until the target is found or no valid range remains.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Binary Search achieves O(log n) average-case and worst-case complexity because the search space halves during every iteration.

The best case is O(1), which occurs when the target is already the middle element. Space complexity is O(1) for iterative implementations because only a few pointer variables are required.

Recursive implementations may consume additional stack memory because recursive calls are stored in memory.

sections.title: Binary Search vs Linear Search
sections.content:
Linear Search checks elements sequentially and works on unsorted data. Binary Search requires sorted data but dramatically improves efficiency through Divide and Conquer.

Linear Search may need to inspect every element, while Binary Search repeatedly removes half of the remaining workload.

This makes Binary Search much more scalable for very large datasets.

sections.title: Recursive Binary Search
sections.content:
Binary Search can also be implemented recursively. Instead of using loops, the function repeatedly calls itself on smaller search ranges.

Each recursive call handles a reduced portion of the array until the target is found or the search range becomes invalid.

Recursive implementations reinforce the idea of recursive decomposition in Divide and Conquer algorithms.

subsections.title: Advantages
bullets: Demonstrates Divide and Conquer thinking clearly.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: Incorrect midpoint logic may cause errors.
Maintaining sorted data may require additional work.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Binary Search appears in databases, search engines, debugging systems, autocomplete systems, compiler optimization, AI search spaces, and version control systems.

Many modern systems rely on Binary Search because logarithmic growth remains efficient even for extremely large datasets.

subsections.title: Mistake: Using Binary Search on unsorted arrays
subsections.content: Binary Search requires ordered data. Without sorting, comparisons cannot safely eliminate sections of the array.

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect midpoint calculation
subsections.content: Poor midpoint logic may create infinite loops, skipped elements, or incorrect search behavior.

subsections.title: Mistake: Forgetting pointer updates
subsections.content: If the low or high pointers are not updated correctly, the search range may never shrink properly.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Binary Search works on sorted arrays.
The algorithm repeatedly divides the search space in half.
Binary Search uses low, high, and mid pointers.
Each comparison removes half of the remaining work.
Binary Search achieves O(log n) efficiency.
Divide and Conquer thinking enables scalable searching.
